claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 forms an initially protective iron-oxide film.
Above approximately 600 °C in a salt-laden environment, the oxide film on Q235 undergoes morphology changes or spallation.
High-temperature oxide-scale morphology changes or spallation accelerate corrosion of Q235.
At or below approximately 600 °C, the oxide layer on Q235 remains adherent and provides relatively stable protection.
Q235 coupons will be exposed sequentially to 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl at 25, 300, 600, and 900 °C while oxide evolution is characterized.
The proposed study uses 100-hour isothermal holds and compares Q235 with a corrosion-resistant reference under identical conditions.
Increasing temperature and salt attack govern growth, densification, and eventual spallation of the iron-based oxide scale.
Moderate temperatures promote formation of a stable protective oxide layer.
At higher temperatures, salt promotes oxide cracking, spallation, or molten-salt infiltration that exposes the substrate.
Exposure of the substrate following scale breakdown produces more aggressive corrosion.
At or below 600 °C, Q235 will exhibit minimal mass loss.
At or below 600 °C, Q235 will develop a relatively thick, adherent oxide scale with stable surface layers.
Above 600 °C, the Q235 oxide scale will spall.
Above 600 °C, Q235 will show rapid mass gain from oxide formation followed by accelerated mass loss.
At high temperature, Q235 will corrode more aggressively than the corrosion-resistant reference.
The selected heat- or corrosion-resistant steel or HEA reference forms a more stable oxide scale with less spallation.
The proposed mechanism applies to carbon steels compositionally similar to Q235 in Na2SO4-NaCl environments.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in very-low-oxygen environments.
Substantial alloying additions may alter oxide formation enough that the proposed mechanism no longer applies.
Scale composition and corrosion kinetics may vary with trace-element content, salt chemistry, and thermal-cycling protocol.
